report:
# Evidence on Chlorhexidine-Alcohol vs. Iodine-Alcohol for Cesarean Skin Preparation

**Conclusion:** The evidence is mixed but leans in favor of chlorhexidine-alcohol, though the claim is not definitively proven across all studies.

## Key Evidence

**Supporting the claim:**
- The largest randomized trial (NEJM, 1,147 patients) found chlorhexidine-alcohol resulted in a **significantly lower** risk of surgical-site infection after cesarean delivery compared to iodine-alcohol (superficial SSI: 3.0% vs. 4.9%; deep: 1.0% vs. 2.4%) [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048].
- A systematic review and meta-analysis concluded chlorhexidine-alcohol **reduces SSI** compared to povidone-iodine solutions [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/].
- An updated meta-analysis found chlorhexidine-containing solutions were superior (RR=0.69, 95% CI 0.54–0.89, p=0.004) [https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2025.1641815/full].

**Not supporting the claim:**
- A pilot RCT (311 women) found fewer SSIs with chlorhexidine-alcohol (5.4% vs. 8.6%) but **not statistically significant** [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/].
- Another RCT found **similar SSI rates** across preparations (povidone-iodine 4.6%, chlorhexidine-alcohol 4.5%, P=.85) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26551196/].
- A network meta-analysis found all credible intervals **overlapped**, though alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of effectiveness [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282].

**Bottom line:** The claim is supported by the largest trial and several meta-analyses, but not all studies reach statistical significance. Your skepticism is partially justified—evidence is inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no significant difference.
